title: Circular motion and gravitation
note: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, toward the center, at a_c = v²/r. Some real force, such as tension, friction, or gravity, must supply this inward net force. Gravity between any two masses follows an inverse-square law, F = Gm₁m₂/r².

read.title: Falling around the Earth
text: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. That centripetal acceleration points toward the center and equals v²/r. By Newton's second law, something must provide a net inward force of mv²/r. For a car on a flat curve it is static friction; for a ball on a string it is tension; for the Moon it is gravity. If the force disappears, the object continues in a straight line tangent to the circle, not straight outward.

Newton realized that the force pulling an apple down is the same force holding the Moon in orbit. Every mass attracts every other mass with a force Gm₁m₂/r². The constant G is tiny, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², which is why we notice gravity only when at least one mass is enormous.

An orbiting spacecraft is not beyond gravity's reach; at the altitude of the International Space Station, gravity is still about 90% of its surface value. The craft is falling toward Earth the whole time, but it moves sideways fast enough that the surface curves away beneath it. Astronauts feel weightless because they fall along with their ship.
